title: How to Get Screened In at SSB
author: Defence Roger
data: A complete guide on clearing the SSB screening process based on personal experience, observations, and discussions with serving officers.
excerpt: Learn what actually matters during the SSB screening process, from OIR and PP&DT to communication, body language, and preparation strategies.

content.text: One of the most common questions I receive is, 'How do I get screened in during the SSB?' Before we begin, let me make one thing very clear. In my opinion, getting screened in is approximately 50% preparation and 50% luck. These are not my own words—I was told this by an ex-psychologist who is now a serving officer. While luck is something none of us can control, the remaining 50% is completely in our hands. This article focuses on that part.
Why Should You Listen to Me?

I am not claiming to know everything about the SSB. However, I have appeared for four SSBs—two for the NDA, one for TES and one for NAVY-TECH. I have never been screened out and have been recommended three times. Although I am currently not in the academy due to medical reasons, I want to help serious aspirants avoid the mistakes that cause many deserving candidates to leave on Day 1.
Understanding the Screening Process

As of August 2026, a few SSB centres have introduced computer-based OIR tests and some procedural changes. However, most centres still follow the traditional Day 1 process consisting of the Officer Intelligence Rating (OIR) Test followed by the Picture Perception and Discussion Test (PP&DT). Understanding how these two stages are evaluated is the first step towards improving your chances.
The OIR Test

The OIR Test consists of two separate booklets, each containing 50 objective questions to be solved in 35 minutes. In total, you attempt 100 questions over two sessions. Some centres now conduct this digitally, but the purpose remains the same—testing your basic reasoning ability under time pressure.

Many candidates believe the OIR score alone decides whether they get screened in. That is not entirely true. Based on discussions with an SSB officer, the OIR score usually acts more like a supporting factor rather than the deciding one. Unless your score is extremely poor, it generally contributes only a small percentage to the final screening decision.
A good OIR score helps, but it rarely compensates for poor performance during the PP&DT discussion.
How to Write a Good PP&DT Story

Many candidates focus entirely on speaking skills and ignore story writing. While communication during the discussion carries significant weight, your written story also contributes to your overall performance. If you are someone who occasionally stutters, hesitates, or feels nervous while speaking in front of a group, a well-written story can strengthen your performance. It may not completely compensate for poor communication, but it certainly helps present your thought process clearly.

Before explaining the structure, let me share something that I found extremely valuable. A serving Army officer, who had previously worked as an Interviewing Officer, once explained to me how stories are generally evaluated. He even showed me the evaluation margins used while checking candidates' stories. Although assessment methods may vary and should never be considered an official marking scheme, the advice he gave regarding story writing has stayed with me and helped me understand what makes a good PP&DT story.

content.text: A Simple Structure That Works

One mistake many candidates make is trying to create an extraordinary story. You do not need to write like a novelist. Keep your story simple, practical and structured. I generally recommend dividing your story into three parts.
Step 1: Write the Introduction

Assume you are shown the picture above. The first two lines should simply explain what you observe in the image. Do not begin with a complicated plot. Introduce the main character and establish the scene. Two lines are generally enough. Writing much more wastes valuable time, while writing too little may fail to explain the situation properly.

For example, I would begin with something like: 'Sohan, a resident of Delhi, visited his ancestral village after a long time. Curious about the local culture, he decided to wear a traditional dhoti-kurta for the first time.' Notice that these two lines simply establish the scene. There is no unnecessary drama or unrealistic storyline.
Step 2: Develop the Story

The next five to eight lines should explain what happens next. One of the easiest ways to write a natural story is by relating the situation to your own experiences. Change the names, modify the situation slightly and adapt your own experiences to the picture.

In the example above, I have never actually worn a dhoti, but I have worn a kurta-pajama. I can use that personal experience to explain how Sohan initially felt uncomfortable, gradually became confident, interacted with the villagers and enjoyed experiencing the traditional lifestyle. These are believable events and make the story sound genuine.
Simple and believable stories almost always leave a better impression than dramatic ones.
Step 3: Write a Short Conclusion

Finish your story with one or two lines that naturally conclude the situation. Do not introduce a completely new event in the ending. Simply summarize the outcome or mention what the character learned from the experience.

content.text: Always Keep Your Story Realistic

Now look at the picture above. Suppose it shows a girl drowning and a boat is visible nearby. Many candidates immediately start writing heroic stories, but that is not what the assessors are looking for. They want to see practical thinking, sound judgement and common sense.

A practical story would explain that the candidate quickly used the nearby boat, threw a rope or used a life jacket to rescue the girl before calling for additional help if required. This demonstrates presence of mind and the ability to make sensible decisions under pressure.

On the other hand, writing that the hero immediately jumped into deep water, carried the girl on his shoulders and swam back to shore without using any available resources sounds unrealistic. In an actual emergency, valuable time would be lost and such actions could endanger both people. Practical solutions are almost always better than cinematic ones.
Don't Try to Be Shakespeare

The assessors are not evaluating your ability to write literature. They want to understand how you think. Whether your story is inspired by a real-life incident or is completely fictional does not matter, provided it is logical, realistic and easy to follow. Keep your language simple, your sequence clear and your ending positive. A straightforward story with practical decisions creates a much stronger impression than an overcomplicated one.
The Importance of Listening Skills

One quality that many candidates completely ignore is listening. Before every stage, the officers provide instructions. Around 90% of these instructions are standard, but the remaining 10% may differ from centre to centre. Missing these small details can leave a poor first impression.

For example, during my first SSB, the officer clearly instructed that nobody was allowed to stand while narrating the group story during the PP&DT discussion. One candidate either missed or ignored this instruction and stood up anyway. The officer immediately pointed it out in front of everyone. Although that candidate eventually got screened in, it demonstrated that he had not listened carefully. Pay close attention whenever the officers are briefing you.
Speaking Skills: The Biggest Deciding Factor
In my experience, the single biggest factor affecting your screening result is your ability to communicate during the group discussion. Notice that I said communication—not English.

You do not need to sound like a native English speaker. You simply need to express your thoughts clearly, confidently, and fluently enough that the people around you understand your ideas. Your voice should be audible without shouting. Speak with confidence, maintain a steady pace, and avoid rushing through your points.

Many capable candidates get screened out simply because they never manage to present their ideas effectively during the discussion. The assessors can only judge what you demonstrate—not what you think.
Body Language Matters

Communication is not limited to words. Your body language also creates an impression. Sit with a straight spine, keep your hands relaxed on your lap, maintain a composed posture, and avoid unnecessary movements. While the officers are briefing the group, maintain attentive eye contact with the speaker. During interactions, carry a natural smile whenever appropriate. It doesn't have to be perfect—it simply reflects confidence and positivity.
Practice the Entire Process

This is probably the most ignored part of SSB preparation. Many candidates study psychology, GTO tasks, and interview questions but never practice speaking in a group of 10 to 15 people. The PP&DT discussion is a completely different environment from speaking alone.

The more you practice discussing stories in a competitive group, the more natural your communication becomes. You learn when to enter the discussion, how to present your ideas without interrupting others unnecessarily, and how to remain calm under pressure.
Should You Join Coaching?

This is a personal decision, but I believe coaching can be beneficial for many candidates—not because it teaches magical techniques, but because it provides structured practice. The biggest advantage is that you repeatedly simulate the actual PP&DT environment with other aspirants.

Even after being recommended, I joined coaching again for additional practice before another attempt. The structured discussions and repeated simulations helped improve my confidence and communication further.

Can you get recommended without coaching? Absolutely. Thousands do every year. However, if you struggle with confidence or group discussions, structured practice may significantly improve your ability to showcase your actual personality.
Final Thoughts

The screening process is not designed to eliminate good candidates—it is designed to identify those who can demonstrate officer-like qualities within a very limited time. Unfortunately, many deserving candidates fail to communicate their true potential and are screened out before reaching the later stages.

Focus on improving the things you can control. Practice OIR questions regularly, listen carefully to every instruction, communicate your ideas clearly, maintain confident body language, and most importantly, practice speaking in a group environment. Preparation cannot eliminate luck, but it can ensure that when the opportunity comes, you are ready to make the best possible impression.
